title: Canada Bars Entry to Foreign Travelers From Congo Over Ebola, Defying WHO Advice
excerpt: Starting July 20, foreigners who visited the Democratic Republic of Congo in the previous 21 days will be denied entry into Canada as the Ebola outbreak crosses 2,100 confirmed cases.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Canada bans entry for foreigners visiting Congo in the last 21 days, effective July 20.
  • The ban contradicts WHO advice, which warns against travel restrictions during outbreaks.
  • Congo's Ebola outbreak has over 2,267 confirmed cases and 893 deaths, marking a significant health crisis.
  • The US has similar entry restrictions for travelers from Congo, affecting American aid workers.
  • Indian travelers may face complications due to Canada's new travel restrictions.
  • Canada will deny entry to any foreign national who visited Congo within the past 21 days, effective Monday, July 20 at 11:59 PM EDT.
  • The ban goes against WHO guidance, which warns that travel restrictions create stigma and can make outbreaks harder to control.
  • Congo's Ebola outbreak has now reached over 2,267 confirmed cases and 893 deaths, making it the third-largest on record.
  • The US already blocks Americans who were recently in Congo from entering via commercial aviation.

New Border Measures Take Effect Monday

Canada's Public Health Agency announced on Sunday that it would deny entry to any foreign national who has been in the Democratic Republic of Congo within the past 21 days, citing the need to reduce public health risks for Canadians. The temporary border measures take effect Monday, July 20 at 11:59 PM EDT.

The 21-day window matches the maximum incubation period for Ebola, during which an infected person could develop symptoms. The virus spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of someone who is infected.

The decision puts Canada in direct conflict with the World Health Organization, which has repeatedly advised against travel or trade restrictions with Congo. The UN health agency argues that such measures create stigma and can actually make epidemics harder to control.

"People from affected regions and African communities have faced unfair suspicion. The spread of Ebola is not determined by nationality or ethnicity."

— World Health Organization

Outbreak Reaches Alarming Scale

The Ebola outbreak in the DRC has reached alarming proportions. As of July 15, Congo had reported more than 2,100 confirmed cases including 828 deaths, according to Reuters. More recent government data puts the toll at 2,267 cases and 893 deaths, with 86 new cases and 29 deaths recorded in a single 24-hour period.

The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, is the third-largest and the fastest-growing on record, according to Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF). The charity warned last week that the epidemic is spreading faster than containment efforts can keep up.

Ongoing conflict in eastern Congo, limited health infrastructure, violence against healthcare workers, and frequent cross-border population movement have all complicated the response.

US Already Imposed Similar Restrictions

Canada's move follows the United States, which last week introduced measures preventing Americans who had been in Congo in the previous 21 days from entering the US via commercial aviation. The CDC has implemented entry screening and restrictions under both Title 42 and Title 49 authorities.

Seven American aid workers who had been working in Congo to combat the outbreak are currently quarantining in a facility in Kenya.

The US has expanded its measures to also screen travelers arriving from Uganda and South Sudan, neighboring countries that face elevated risk of cross-border transmission.

What This Means for Indian Travelers

The travel ban adds another layer of complexity for Indian nationals who may transit through or travel to Canada. While direct travel between India and Congo is minimal, Indians working in African countries or those transiting through affected regions could find themselves caught by the 21-day rule.

Canada remains one of the top destinations for Indian students and workers. The Public Health Agency's measures do not apply to Canadian citizens or permanent residents, but could affect the estimated 900,000 Indian students and temporary workers currently in the country if they have recently traveled to the DRC.

India has not imposed similar travel restrictions related to the Ebola outbreak, though the country has separately ordered its 300,000 seafarers to avoid the Strait of Hormuz due to the separate US-Iran conflict.
